fixes.explanation: Moses is the one hearing the LORD's instructions, but he isn't named for this bull. The verse says Aaron makes atonement “…for himself and his household.” (Leviticus 16:6). It's Aaron's bull and Aaron's household. Moses' household isn't on that list.

The incense has its own job, baker. It goes on the fire so the cloud covers the mercy seat (Leviticus 16:13). The goat's blood is sprinkled “…against the mercy seat and in front of it.” (Leviticus 16:15). The text gives the incense one job and the blood another, and it never mixes them.

I see why you'd think big, friend, but this verse keeps it close to home. The reason is “…the impurities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins.” (Leviticus 16:16). The neighbors never get named. Even the Most Holy Place gets atonement because of the Israelites' sins, and that's the whole list.

Yes, baker. Aaron sprinkles the blood on it seven times “…to cleanse it and consecrate it from the uncleanness of the Israelites.” (Leviticus 16:19). The altar gets cleansed and consecrated. Earlier, Aaron also makes atonement for the Most Holy Place and the Tent of Meeting (Leviticus 16:16), and the altar is part of that same day's work.

That's right, baker. Aaron lays both hands on the live goat's head and confesses over it “…all the iniquities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins.” (Leviticus 16:21). Then he puts them on the goat's head and sends it away by the hand of a man appointed for the task. I think this is a serious moment, and the text treats it that way.

A lamb? Baker, I like the creativity, but I checked the whole animal list in this chapter. It has a bull, goats and rams, and no lamb. Verse 24 says Aaron sacrifices “…his burnt offering and the people’s burnt offering to make atonement for himself and for the people.” Other priests aren't mentioned there at all.

That's right, baker. The man who released the goat “…must wash his clothes and bathe himself with water; afterward he may reenter the camp.” (Leviticus 16:26). Both the washing and the bath come before he's back in. Walking a goat out to a solitary place is a job that ends with laundry.

No waiting period in this verse, friend. The text says he “…must wash his clothes and bathe himself with water; afterward he may reenter the camp.” (Leviticus 16:26). The thing that comes before reentering is the washing and the bath. No number of days is given.

You got it, baker. The bull and the goat are taken outside the camp, “and their hides, flesh, and dung must be burned up.” (Leviticus 16:27). The verse names all three: hides, flesh and dung. All of it goes up in fire.

The text doesn't hand any of it to the priests, baker. It says the bull and the goat are taken outside the camp, “and their hides, flesh, and dung must be burned up.” (Leviticus 16:27). Hides, flesh and dung are the things it names for burning. Priests aren't mentioned in that verse.

Enrich is a nice word, baker, and it does sound like a Monday goal. But the verse says, “…you shall humble yourselves and not do any work…” (Leviticus 16:29). The day is for humbling, and the people don't work. The word is humble.

Leaving Egypt is a big day too, friend, but it's not the reason here. The LORD says, “…on this day atonement will be made for you to cleanse you…” (Leviticus 16:30). This chapter never mentions Egypt. The day is big because of the cleansing, and that's the answer.

I see where that comes from, baker. Seven times does show up in this chapter, with the blood sprinkled before the mercy seat (Leviticus 16:14) and on the altar (Leviticus 16:19). But the statute is about how often the atonement happens. The LORD says, “…to make atonement once a year for the Israelites because of all their sins.” (Leviticus 16:34).
